title: Malignant Hypertension: The Ocular Emergency
summary: Malignant Hypertension (Grade IV Hypertensive Retinopathy) is a medical emergency defined by severe arterial hypertension (>180/120 mmHg) associated with multi-organ damage, most notably bilateral optic disc edema. It represents a total breakdown of ocular autoregulation and requires immediate, controlled systemic intervention.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Malignant hypertension is the most severe form of hypertensive retinopathy (KWB Grade IV). It is characterized by accelerated microvascular damage leading to fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles. Clinically, the hallmark is bilateral papilledema in the presence of severely elevated blood pressure, often accompanied by encephalopathy, renal failure, or cardiac decompensation.

rows: Grade I + Focal narrowing and Arteriovenous (AV) nipping
Grade II + Flame hemorrhages, CWS, and hard exudates

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Bilateral Optic Disc Edema (blurred margins, hyperemia)
Flame-shaped Hemorrhages (nerve fiber layer layer)
Cotton Wool Spots (infarcts of the pre-capillary arterioles)
Hard Exudates in a 'Macular Star' pattern (Henle's layer)
Elschnig Spots (yellow-black spots representing choroidal infarcts)
Siegrist Streaks (linear hyperpigmentation along choroidal vessels)
Serous Retinal Detachment (due to severe choroidal ischemia)

sections.title: Systemic Red Flags
content: Hypertensive Encephalopathy (Confusion, Seizures)
Acute Renal Failure (Oliguria, Azotemia)
Acute Left Ventricular Failure (Pulmonary Edema)
Dissecting Aortic Aneurysm
Eclampsia (in pregnant patients)
Intracranial Hemorrhage

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: Step 1: Immediate BP Measurement (bilateral arms) and Pulse Oximetry.
Step 2: Dilated Fundus Exam (DFE) - Look for disc edema and macular star.
Step 3: Bloods - Urea, Electrolytes, Creatinine, Cardiac Enzymes, Urinalysis (Proteinuria).
Step 4: Imaging - OCT Macula (to quantify SRF) and Head CT/MRI if neurological signs present.
Step 5: Fluorescein Angiogram (FFA) - Shows multiple leakage points and capillary non-perfusion (rarely done in acute phase).

rows: Microaneurysms; No disc edema unless papillopathy
BP is normal; patient often young/obese female
Unilateral; Viral prodrome; Optic nerve inflammation
Altitudinal field defect; Pale disc edema; Normal BP

sections.title: Emergency Management Protocol
content: 1. Admission to ICU/HDU for continuous monitoring.
2. Controlled BP Reduction: Aim for 10-20% reduction in Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) in first hour.
3. Targeted BP: Lower to 160/100-110 mmHg over the next 2-6 hours.
4. Avoid Precipitous Drops: Prevents watershed cerebral/optic nerve infarction.
5. Transition to Oral Meds: Over 24-48 hours once stabilized.

rows: 20mg IV bolus initially; avoid in Asthma/CHF
Short-acting; good for aortic dissection cases

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: The presence of macular star is a sign of chronicity (at least 1-2 weeks of edema).
Always check BP in every patient presenting with bilateral disc swelling or 'unexplained' retinal hemorrhages.
Elschnig spots are pathognomonic for hypertensive choroidopathy and indicate severe acute rise in BP.
Wait 4-6 weeks after BP stabilization before performing laser or injections if macular edema persists.
Rapid reduction of BP can cause NAION-like optic nerve infarction due to loss of perfusion pressure.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Evidence
sections.content: The SPRINT trial emphasized intensive BP control (<120 mmHg systolic) for reducing cardiovascular events, but in the acute 'Malignant' phase, the JNC-8 and AHA guidelines still caution against rapid lowering to avoid autoregulatory failure in the brain and eye. Modern OCT-Angiography (OCT-A) now allows us to visualize the Deep Capillary Plexus (DCP) ischemia which correlates better with final visual acuity than surface hemorrhages.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Usually secondary to renal parenchymal disease (e.g., Glomerulonephritis).
May present with vague symptoms like irritability or headache.
Pheochromocytoma must be ruled out in children with malignant HTN.
Neuroblastoma can occasionally mimic hypertensive crises.
